data.title: D1 v1: client creation (server) — the POST /clients nobody owns

data.to:
Gap found while planning AS-42 (cto-owen, 2026-09-02) and independently confirmed by the orchestrator: repos.clients.create has ZERO non-test callers. Twenty call sites exist, all in test files. AS-39 built the repository; AS-43 and AS-42 both accept a clientId and neither creates one. Nothing in the shipped application can bring a client into existence.

WHY IT FELL THROUGH. The milestone plan cut the Clients screen (row C-16) precisely BECAUSE clients are created inline from the invoice and contract screens. That reasoning is sound for the UI, but it left the server half owned by nobody: AS-39 stopped at the repository, and the two consumers each assumed the other end existed. The boundary filter did its job on the screen and the split between server and UI tasks lost the endpoint.

WHY IT BLOCKS. AS-47's empty-client state is reached on the very first contract a freelancer creates — Flow 1 step 8 — and AS-46's invoice screen has the same inline-create affordance. Both UI tasks will arrive at a server that cannot answer them.

DECISION ALREADY RECORDED, to be confirmed in planning (AS-42 plan section 11): ONE shared POST /clients, built once, used by both screens. Never two endpoints, and never folded into POST /contracts or POST /invoices as a nested create — a nested create makes client creation a side effect of a different resource and makes partial failure ambiguous. The default is that whichever of AS-46 or AS-47 lands first builds it; filing it separately here instead means neither UI task carries a hidden server dependency and the endpoint gets its own review.

SHAPE, for the planner rather than binding: the route sits below the auth boundary and takes its freelancer from the session, exactly as AS-42 and AS-43 do; ownership is enforced by the composite FK rather than re-checked in application code; the repository already enforces name and email validation and is already tested (AS-39 cases cover create, uniqueness semantics, and the FK). The plan should say what happens on a duplicate — AS-39 deliberately did NOT make client email unique per freelancer (see the states ledger), so duplicates are legal and the answer is probably to return the new row rather than to converge on an existing one, but that is a decision to take and record, not to assume.

ACCEPTANCE: the description's shape holds; ownership is engine-enforced and a cross-tenant attempt returns the same answer as a nonexistent parent; at least one falsification recipe breaks a guard this task introduces, shown red once per the house technique (assert the mutation applied on disk and in the built image, predict executable case names that exist, restore, prove restoration by content hash plus git status --porcelain, rebuild before re-running); the test service stays network_mode: none; no new dependencies; no migration (the table exists); no protected top-level file edited; no running container touched. Complexity low.

Pulled as the top D1 pull: it is the only remaining high, its dependency (AS-40) is done, and it directly blocks AS-46 and AS-47 — the two UI screens that both create clients inline. Every other remaining D1 task is a UI task or the acceptance run.

Lena implements. Marcus wrote AS-42 and AS-43, the two consumers that take a clientId and assume this endpoint exists, so a fresh reader is more likely to notice if the endpoint's shape quietly diverges from what they assumed. She also built the auth boundary this route sits below.

Note for the planner, and it is the whole reason this task exists as a separate one: AS-39 built the clients repository and nothing ever called it. The endpoint fell between the repository task and the two UI tasks and was owned by neither. So the plan should state, explicitly, which task owns each half of a resource whose creation surface is split across a screen and a server — that boundary is what failed here, and AS-46/AS-47 will hit the same seam for anything else they create inline.

Plan written. Duplicate ruling: POST /clients unconditionally inserts and never converges — the schema declines the unique index on purpose (0001-initial.js: 'NOT unique: duplicate is a non-blocking warning') and the ledger requires 'create a new client anyway' to be an expressible outcome, which an upsert cannot express; a double submit therefore creates two rows, accepted, with no money and no external call behind it. Response is 303 to a REQUIRED, safeNext-validated return path carrying clientId=<new id> — required rather than defaulted because there is no Clients screen to default to and a default would silently discard the form the freelancer was filling. The route adds nothing the repository already does: no field allowlist (assertKnownKeys is the one that cannot be bypassed), no name/email check, no length ceiling. Ownership is actingFreelancerId as the first positional argument and the composite FK; there is no cross-tenant path INTO this route, which is stated and proven rather than papered over with an unreachable 404 mapping. Five falsification recipes, F1 falsifies the ownership scoping and F5 gives the composite FK the recipe it has been missing since AS-42. Also filed AS-67: client email format validation is missing one layer down and belongs in the repository, not smuggled into this route — which is the same seam rule this task exists to write.

Recording the §3.7 rule as a standing convention proposal rather than leaving it inside one task's plan, because it is the only artifact from this task that outlives it.

The rule: a resource whose creation surface is split between a screen and a server has three obligations with three owners — the row (the repository task), the ENDPOINT (a task of its own, filed when the repository task lands), and the states (the screen task). The endpoint is never inherited by "whichever screen gets there first". That default is exactly what produced this gap: two screens each assumed the other carried it, and the endpoint was owned by neither for four tasks.

The mechanical test is the part worth keeping, because it is checkable rather than exhortative: a repository write method with zero non-test callers at the end of its own task is an unowned endpoint, not a finished repository. Grep before done; every zero-caller method either names a filed consumer task or gets one filed.

Applying the test right now, to this codebase, finds a second instance: repos.clients.update still has zero non-test callers after AS-65 lands, and no consumer task exists anywhere in the screen budget. Owen raised it and deliberately did not action it — that is a CTO call he would rather make with AS-46 and AS-47 planned, which is the right sequencing. THE PARSED BODY'S PROTOTYPE — THE PLAN'S §3.4 LOAD-BEARING NOTE IS WRONG, AND THE DESIGN IS UNCHANGED ANYWAY.
Probed inside the real image (express 5.2.1, body-parser 2.3.0, node 24.20.0) rather than taken on trust, POSTing a real urlencoded form through `express.urlencoded({ extended: false, limit: '32kb', parameterLimit: 20 })`:
  Object.getPrototypeOf(req.body) === Object.prototype  ->  TRUE
  Object.getPrototypeOf(req.body) === null              ->  FALSE
  assertPlainObject(req.body, 'raw')                    ->  ACCEPTED
So the body is NOT null-prototype and passing it straight to the repository would NOT 400 for that reason. Mechanism, read off the shipped source: body-parser 2.3.0's createQueryParser routes BOTH extended and non-extended through `qs.parse` (lib/types/urlencoded.js:99) — `extended: false` only sets `depth: 0`; it no longer uses node:querystring at all, and qs with `plainObjects` unset builds with `{}`. The plan's inference was correct for the older body-parser that did use querystring.parse.
The rest-spread stays, for the reason the plan gives independently: `next` is the router's field and must be split out or the repository's assertKnownKeys rejects it. That is what L1 actually catches — it 400s on `client.next`, not on the prototype. Second probe, worth knowing: with NO content-type the parser does not run and `req.body` is `undefined`, which is why the handler reads `req.body ?? {}`.

=============================================================================
1. DEFECT (blocking) — POST /clients emits a PROTOCOL-RELATIVE Location for
   inputs safeNext accepts. This is a live open redirect, and the URL
   composition is its sole mechanism.
=============================================================================
REPRODUCTION (live, through the built image, signed-in session, valid Origin):

  POST /clients   name=C&email=c@example.test&next=%2F.%2F%2Fevil.test
  -> 303  Location: //evil.test?clientId=8f186329-4bdb-4927-8259-140318ffdb05

A browser resolves that Location as a network-path reference: the freelancer
lands on http://evil.test, and the id just minted for them goes with it in the
query. 10 of my 27 vectors escaped the app origin. The escaping classes:

  /.//evil.test               -> //evil.test                  => http://evil.test
  /..//evil.test              -> //evil.test                  => http://evil.test
  /%2e//evil.test             -> //evil.test                  => http://evil.test
  /%2E%2E//evil.test          -> //evil.test                  => http://evil.test
  /a/..//evil.test            -> //evil.test                  => http://evil.test
  /.//user:pass@evil.test/x   -> //user:pass@evil.test/x       => http://evil.test  (credential)
  /.//evil.test:8080/x        -> //evil.test:8080/x            => http://evil.test:8080
  /.//evil.test/path?a=b#frag -> //evil.test/path?a=b&clientId=...#frag
  /.//                        -> //?clientId=...               (Location that will not parse)

Held (all 400, correctly, at safeNext): absolute `https://evil.test/x`;
protocol-relative `//evil.test/x`; backslash `/\evil.test/x`, `\\evil.test`;
schemes `javascript:`, `data:`, `mailto:`, `http:evil.test`; CRLF
`/x\r\nSet-Cookie: a=b` and `/x\nLocation: https://evil.test`; TAB and NUL;
`://` in the query. Held and stayed app-relative through composition:
`/....//evil.test`, `/%2f/evil.test`, `/;/evil.test`, `/.%2f/evil.test`.

THE ANSWER TO THE QUESTION THE PLAN RAISED AND DID NOT SETTLE — HOW MANY
LAYERS ACTUALLY STOP AN OPEN REDIRECT HERE.
  Exactly ONE: safeNext. And for this class, ZERO.
  The composition step is not a second layer, and it is not merely a mask. It
  is a NEGATIVE layer: it manufactures the escape. Measured both ways on the
  same values, emitting each as a raw Location and as the composed one:

    next                 raw Location -> origin           composed -> origin
    /.//evil.test        /.//evil.test -> APP ORIGIN      //evil.test -> http://evil.test
    /..//evil.test       /..//evil.test -> APP ORIGIN     //evil.test -> http://evil.test
    /%2e//evil.test      /%2e//evil.test -> APP ORIGIN    //evil.test -> http://evil.test
    /a/..//evil.test     /a/..//evil.test -> APP ORIGIN   //evil.test -> http://evil.test
    /.//evil.test/p?a=b  -> APP ORIGIN                    //evil.test/p -> http://evil.test
    /invoices/new        -> APP ORIGIN                    /invoices/new?clientId=ID -> APP ORIGIN

  RFC 3986 §5 decides "is this a network-path reference" on the RAW reference
  BEFORE dot-segment removal, so `/.//evil.test` sent as-is is path-absolute and
  stays same-origin. `new URL(next, base).pathname` performs that removal and
  hands back `//evil.test`, which re-emitted standalone IS a network-path
  reference. Every one of these vectors is safe until landing() touches it.
